dct_description_sm: The ecological role of thaw ponds (thermokarst ponds and other arctic ponds associated with permafrost active layer) on carbon cycling is now a major concern among polar scientists, as they can represent a significant source of carbon to the atmosphere. In several Polar Regions, thawing of permafrost has generated an increasing number of ponds that can act as gas conduits to the atmosphere. Arctic and subarctic soils contain a large pool of carbon accumulated over thousands of years, which is now made available to microbial and photochemical degradation once it's liberated to the aquatic systems. These two processes produce greenhouse gases (GHG) that are transferred to the atmosphere at unknown rates, depending on several limnological factors (e.g., thermal structure, anoxy, DOM, organic matter lability). Some of this carbon can also be transferred to the aquatic network and eventually to coastal zones of the ocean. Both of these transfers may significantly affect the global carbon budget. The objectives of this research program are: 1- Measure GHG emissions from thaw ponds in the Subarctic (inferior limit of discontinuous permafrost) and Arctic (Bylot Island; continuous permafrost), 2- Investigate what controls GHG emission rates (e.g., microbial assemblages and activity, temperature, DOM photolysis, physical factors), 3- Determine the source of the emitted C using optical tools, stable isotopes and 14C dating, 4- Study microbial diversity in these systems, 5- Upscale GHG emission estimates with satellite imagery.
dct_title_s: Limnology of arctic thaw ponds and their greenhouse gas emissions (Bylot Island, Nunavut)
